[[](https://www.google.com/husni.saleh) husni.saleh 53.7K If you’re in Florence and only have time for one museum, trust me, this is the one. It’s called Galleria degli Uffizi.. and this isn’t just a museum. This is where the Renaissance basically leveled up. The building was commissioned in 1560 by the powerful Medici family. It was originally meant to be government offices “Uffizi” literally means offices, but because the Medici family were serious art collectors, it eventually became a gallery filled with their private masterpieces. And the collection? Crazy! It’s huge. It includes paintings by Sandro Botticelli, Andrea del Verrocchio, Filippo Lippi, Raffaello Sanzio, and even early works by Leonardo da Vinci (before the Mona Lisa, but the detail is already next level). Then there are early works by Leonardo da Vinci, including Annunciation. It may not be the Mona Lisa, but you can already see his genius in the composition and subtle details. And here’s something many people don’t know: the Uffizi houses Doni Tondo, the only surviving panel painting by Michelangelo. We usually think of him as the sculptor of David, but this proves he was just as powerful with a brush. You’ll also find dramatic, intense works by Caravaggio.. darker, moodier, totally different vibe. What blows my mind is that this used to be a private family collection. Imagine having all of this as your home decor. Walking through the Uffizi feels like scrolling through a 15th-century masterpiece feed. Tiring? Yes. Overwhelming?Definitely. Worth it? A hundred percent. So if you’re in Florence, don’t just take photos outside. Step inside the Uffizi, and stand face to face with art that literally changed the world. [[](https://www.google.com/husni.saleh) husni.saleh 53.7K If you’re in Florence and only have time for one museum, trust me, this is the one. It’s called Galleria degli Uffizi.. and this isn’t just a museum. This is where the Renaissance basically leveled up. The building was commissioned in 1560 by the powerful Medici family. It was originally meant to be government offices “Uffizi” literally means offices, but because the Medici family were serious art collectors, it eventually became a gallery filled with their private masterpieces. And the collection? Crazy! It’s huge. It includes paintings by Sandro Botticelli, Andrea del Verrocchio, Filippo Lippi, Raffaello Sanzio, and even early works by Leonardo da Vinci (before the Mona Lisa, but the detail is already next level). Then there are early works by Leonardo da Vinci, including Annunciation. It may not be the Mona Lisa, but you can already see his genius in the composition and subtle details. And here’s something many people don’t know: the Uffizi houses Doni Tondo, the only surviving panel painting by Michelangelo. We usually think of him as the sculptor of David, but this proves he was just as powerful with a brush. You’ll also find dramatic, intense works by Caravaggio.. darker, moodier, totally different vibe. What blows my mind is that this used to be a private family collection. Imagine having all of this as your home decor. Walking through the Uffizi feels like scrolling through a 15th-century masterpiece feed. Tiring? Yes. Overwhelming?Definitely. Worth it? A hundred percent. So if you’re in Florence, don’t just take photos outside. Step inside the Uffizi, and stand face to face with art that literally changed the world. Trust me, this place hits different. #florenceitaly #uffizigallery #artloversid #travelreels #museumvibes](https://www.google.com/reel/DVTRp69ifBb/?utm_source=popular_topic_grid)

362 Las “Setas de Sevilla” es uno de los lugares más famosos y curiosos de la ciudad. Su nombre real es Metropol Parasol, pero casi todo el mundo las llama simplemente Las Setas. ✅ Qué son exactamente Es una estructura gigante de madera ubicada en la Plaza de la Encarnación, en el centro histórico de Seville. Fue diseñada por el arquitecto alemán Jürgen Mayer H. y se inauguró en 2011. ✅ Tiene aproximadamente: • 150 m de largo • 70 m de ancho • 26 m de alto Y está considerada la estructura de madera más grande del mundo. ✅ Por qué se llaman “Setas” La forma del techo parece hongos gigantes, por eso los sevillanos empezaron a llamarlas “Las Setas”, y el nombre se volvió tan popular que terminó siendo oficial. ✅ Qué hay dentro El lugar tiene varios niveles con cosas diferentes: 1. Subterráneo: museo arqueológico con restos romanos y árabes llamados Antiquarium. 2. Planta baja: mercado tradicional y restaurantes. 3. Plaza pública: espacio para eventos y actividades. 4. Pasarela arriba: un mirador panorámico desde donde se ve toda la ciudad. ✅ Algo curioso Cuando lo construyeron hubo mucha polémica. • Algunos sevillanos lo aman porque es moderno. • Otros dicen que no combina con la arquitectura antigua de Sevilla. Pero hoy en día es uno de los sitios más fotografiados de la ciudad 📸. 💡 Dato interesante: de noche las Setas se iluminan y hay un paseo arriba que parece una pasarela futurista.

362 Las “Setas de Sevilla” es uno de los lugares más famosos y curiosos de la ciudad. Su nombre real es Metropol Parasol, pero casi todo el mundo las llama simplemente Las Setas. ✅ Qué son exactamente Es una estructura gigante de madera ubicada en la Plaza de la Encarnación, en el centro histórico de Seville. Fue diseñada por el arquitecto alemán Jürgen Mayer H. y se inauguró en 2011. ✅ Tiene aproximadamente: • 150 m de largo • 70 m de ancho • 26 m de alto Y está considerada la estructura de madera más grande del mundo. ✅ Por qué se llaman “Setas” La forma del techo parece hongos gigantes, por eso los sevillanos empezaron a llamarlas “Las Setas”, y el nombre se volvió tan popular que terminó siendo oficial. ✅ Qué hay dentro El lugar tiene varios niveles con cosas diferentes: 1. Subterráneo: museo arqueológico con restos romanos y árabes llamados Antiquarium. 2. Planta baja: mercado tradicional y restaurantes. 3. Plaza pública: espacio para eventos y actividades. 4. Pasarela arriba: un mirador panorámico desde donde se ve toda la ciudad. ✅ Algo curioso Cuando lo construyeron hubo mucha polémica. • Algunos sevillanos lo aman porque es moderno. • Otros dicen que no combina con la arquitectura antigua de Sevilla. Pero hoy en día es uno de los sitios más fotografiados de la ciudad 📸. 💡 Dato interesante: de noche las Setas se iluminan y hay un paseo arriba que parece una pasarela futurista.

It was originally meant to be government offices “Uffizi” literally means offices, but because the Medici family were serious art collectors, it eventually became a gallery filled with their private masterpieces. And the collection? Crazy! It’s huge. It includes paintings by Sandro Botticelli, Andrea del Verrocchio, Filippo Lippi, Raffaello Sanzio, and even early works by Leonardo da Vinci (before the Mona Lisa, but the detail is already next level). Then there are early works by Leonardo da Vinci, including Annunciation. It may not be the Mona Lisa, but you can already see his genius in the composition and subtle details. And here’s something many people don’t know: the Uffizi houses Doni Tondo, the only surviving panel painting by Michelangelo. We usually think of him as the sculptor of David, but this proves he was just as powerful with a brush. You’ll also find dramatic, intense works by Caravaggio.. darker, moodier, totally different vibe. What blows my mind is that this used to be a private family collection. Imagine having all of this as your home decor. Walking through the Uffizi feels like scrolling through a 15th-century masterpiece feed. Tiring? Yes. Overwhelming?Definitely. Worth it? [[](https://www.google.com/husni.saleh) husni.saleh 53.7K If you’re in Florence and only have time for one museum, trust me, this is the one. It’s called Galleria degli Uffizi.. and this isn’t just a museum. This is where the Renaissance basically leveled up. The building was commissioned in 1560 by the powerful Medici family. It was originally meant to be government offices “Uffizi” literally means offices, but because the Medici family were serious art collectors, it eventually became a gallery filled with their private masterpieces. And the collection? Crazy! It’s huge. It includes paintings by Sandro Botticelli, Andrea del Verrocchio, Filippo Lippi, Raffaello Sanzio, and even early works by Leonardo da Vinci (before the Mona Lisa, but the detail is already next level). Then there are early works by Leonardo da Vinci, including Annunciation. It may not be the Mona Lisa, but you can already see his genius in the composition and subtle details. And here’s something many people don’t know: the Uffizi houses Doni Tondo, the only surviving panel painting by Michelangelo. We usually think of him as the sculptor of David, but this proves he was just as powerful with a brush. You’ll also find dramatic, intense works by Caravaggio.. darker, moodier, totally different vibe. What blows my mind is that this used to be a private family collection. Imagine having all of this as your home decor. Walking through the Uffizi feels like scrolling through a 15th-century masterpiece feed. Tiring? Yes. Overwhelming?Definitely. Worth it? A hundred percent. So if you’re in Florence, don’t just take photos outside. Step inside the Uffizi, and stand face to face with art that literally changed the world. The first town in England to become a Cittaslow city (and the first in the English-speaking world) was Ludlow[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-Waking_up-10) in November 2003;[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-research_themes_118-18) the first in Wales was Mold.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-research_themes_118-18) There are currently three towns in the UK that are members.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-uktowns-19)_[Disagrees with five named in the list._]
Pijao, a small town in Colombia, is to become the first Cittaslow city in Latin America.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-20)
Polish Cittaslow towns participate in the annual Cittaslow Towns Festival, hosted each year by a different member town in Poland.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-21) The first festival took place in 2010 in Reszel.
Some localitites withdrew from the organization, including Diss, UK, Fairfax, California, US, Ludlow, UK, Perth, UK, Taraklı, Turkey, and Wydminy, Poland.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-24)

Title: The Fountain Inn Museum
Chunks: 0
**Touching our past**“A people without knowledge of their history, origin and culture is like a tree without roots.”
–_Marcus Garvey_
The goal of the Fountain Inn Museum is to provide all visitors, especially young people, with a clear view of our town’s fascinating past, from its humble beginnings and dynamic growth that led to the futuristic prospects now within sight. A secure footing in our history will enable tomorrow’s leaders to take on the unique challenges of the 21st century.
The museum opened its doors in 2010, part of Fountain Inn’s Commerce Park project in downtown renewal. From the beginning, the aim was to accurately chronicle the town’s inception as a way station on the Charleston/North Carolina stagecoach route, and mark its progress from a mostly farming population to the high tech and manufacturing concerns that dot its landscape today.
An appreciation of Fountain Inn’s history includes exhibits reflecting the time when native Americans inhabited the upstate, grew corn and hunted the game that was plentiful in the Piedmont.
As European settlers began to arrive, roads and buildings soon followed, establishing communities that grew into towns such as Fountain Inn. Museum exhibits and hands-on displays take visitors on a chronological tour of our city’s growth, clearly illustrating the special Fountain Inn heritage.
The museum offers innovative programs and tours for student groups from elementary school through high school. Special events and varying presentations provide great interest even for repeat guests.
The Hooked on History series features programs such as Civil War stories that involved Fountain Inn citizen/soldiers; folk music of the textile belt with live performances; and An Evening with Robert Quillen, the internationally recognized author and publisher of The Fountain Inn Tribune.

Title: 12K views · 184 reactions | Lascaux is a famous network of prehistoric caves in southwestern France, best known for containing some of the most extraordinary examples of Paleolithic cave art ever discovered. The caves lie near the village of Montignac in the Vézère Valley and contain hundreds of paintings and engravings created by humans during the Upper Paleolithic period roughly 17,000–22,000 years ago.  

The cave walls and ceilings are covered with over 600 paintings and around 1,500 engravings, mostly depicting animals that lived in the region during the Ice Age. Despite the huge number of animals depicted, there is only one clear human figure, a mysterious bird-headed man shown in a dramatic scene with a bison.  

The paintings were made using mineral pigments such as charcoal and iron oxides to create colours like black, red, yellow, and brown. Artists sometimes painted directly onto limestone walls or used natural contours of the cave to give the animals a sense of depth and motion. Some figures were also engraved into the rock. The techniques and composition show that prehistoric humans had sophisticated artistic skills and planning.  

Lascaux Cave was discovered accidentally on 12 September 1940 when a teenager named Marcel Ravidat followed his dog into a hole in the ground with three friends. Inside they found the vast decorated chambers, which soon became one of the most important archaeological discoveries of the 20th century. Archaeologists later studied the site extensively, recognizing it as one of the finest examples of prehistoric art in the world.  

The cave was opened to the public in 1948, but heavy tourism quickly began damaging the artwork. Artificial lighting and human breath caused algae growth and fading pigments, so the cave was closed in 1963 to preserve it. Today, visitors cannot enter the original cave. 

In 1979, Lascaux became part of the UNESCO World Heritage listed prehistoric sites.

# Lascaux is a famous network of prehistoric caves in southwestern France, best known for containing some of the most extraordinary examples of Paleolithic cave art ever discovered. The caves lie near the village of Montignac in the Vézère Valley and contain hundreds of paintings and engravings created by humans during the Upper Paleolithic period roughly 17,000–22,000 years ago. The cave walls and ceilings are covered with over 600 paintings and around 1,500 engravings, mostly depicting animals that lived in the region during the Ice Age. Despite the huge number of animals depicted, there is only one clear human figure, a mysterious bird-headed man shown in a dramatic scene with a bison. The paintings were made using mineral pigments such as charcoal and iron oxides to create colours like black, red, yellow, and brown. Artists sometimes painted directly onto limestone walls or used natural contours of the cave to give the animals a sense of depth and motion. Some figures were also engraved into the rock. The techniques and composition show that prehistoric humans had sophisticated artistic skills and planning. Lascaux Cave was discovered accidentally on 12 September 1940 when a teenager named Marcel Ravidat followed his dog into a hole in the ground with three friends. Inside they found the vast decorated chambers, which soon became one of the most important archaeological discoveries of the 20th century. Archaeologists later studied the site extensively, recognizing it as one of the finest examples of prehistoric art in the world. The cave was opened to the public in 1948, but heavy tourism quickly began damaging the artwork. Artificial lighting and human breath caused algae growth and fading pigments, so the cave was closed in 1963 to preserve it. Today, visitors cannot enter the original cave. In 1979, Lascaux became part of the UNESCO World Heritage listed prehistoric sites. #history #iceage #art | Weird History Facts & Vintage Photography | Facebook

**Cittaslow** is an organisation founded in Italy and inspired by the slow food movement. Cittaslow's goals include improving the quality of life in towns by slowing down its overall pace, especially in a city's use of spaces and the flow of life and traffic through them.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-7)
As of November 2025, Cittaslow has 308 members, 221 in Europe, 71 in Asia, 6 in North America, 4 in South America, 4 in Oceania, and 2 in Africa. Countries with most members are Italy (90), Poland (37), Turkey (28), Germany (24), China (18), South Korea (15), France (13) and Spain (11).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-list-1)

Cittaslow was founded in Italy in October 1999, following a meeting organised by the mayor of Greve in Chianti, Tuscany.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-small_town_43-8) A 54-point charter was developed, encouraging high quality local food and drink, general conviviality and the opposition to cultural standardisation.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-small_town_43-8) In 2001, 28 Italian towns were signed up to the pledge, certified by trained operatives of Cittaslow.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-small_town_44-9)
The first Slow City in the English-speaking world was Ludlow, England, in 2003.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-Waking_up-10) In 2004, Reszel became the first Polish town to join Cittaslow, and several soon followed with the number growing to 12 by September 2013 and to 37 by November 2025, making Poland the country with the second highest number of member towns (after Italy).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-mkkg-11)
Welcome sign in Midden-Delfland, Netherlands, containing the Cittaslow logo. Midden-Delfland in 2008 was the first Dutch municipality to join[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-12)
The movement expanded broadly beyond Italy and, by 2006, national Cittaslow networks existed in Germany, Norway and the United Kingdom. In March 2007 the South Australian town of Goolwa was declared a Cittaslow member and became the first Non-European to gain Cittaslow membership_[citation needed_]. By 2007, several slow cities had been introduced across South Korea.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-13)

By mid-2009, fourteen countries had at least one officially accredited Cittaslow community. In July 2009, the small seaside village of Cowichan Bay in Canada became the North American continent's first Cittaslow town._[citation needed_] In June 2011, Gökçeada in Turkey became the first and only Cittaslow island.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-14) As of September 2013, Cittaslow had 177 members, the most in Italy (73), Poland, South Korea, Germany (12 each), Turkey (9) and France (8).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-mkkg-11)
In October 2020, Izmir, Turkey's 3rd metropolitan municipality, has become The First Cittaslow Metropolis of the World.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-15)
Cittaslow sign in Orneta, Poland
There are three categories of membership: Cittaslow town (population less than 50,000); Cittaslow Supporter (population more than 50,000);[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-16) and Cittaslow Friend (individual or family).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-17)
Like Slow Food, Cittaslow is a membership organisation. Full membership of Cittaslow is only open to towns with a population under 50,000. To become eligible for membership, a town must normally score at least 50 percent in a self-assessment process against the set of Cittaslow goals, and then apply for admission to the appropriate Cittaslow national network. An annual membership fee is payable by towns._[citation needed_]

The first town in England to become a Cittaslow city (and the first in the English-speaking world) was Ludlow[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-Waking_up-10) in November 2003;[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-research_themes_118-18) the first in Wales was Mold.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-research_themes_118-18) There are currently three towns in the UK that are members.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-uktowns-19)_[Disagrees with five named in the list._]
Pijao, a small town in Colombia, is to become the first Cittaslow city in Latin America.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-20)
Polish Cittaslow towns participate in the annual Cittaslow Towns Festival, hosted each year by a different member town in Poland.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-21) The first festival took place in 2010 in Reszel.
Some localitites withdrew from the organization, including Diss, UK, Fairfax, California, US, Ludlow, UK, Perth, UK, Taraklı, Turkey, and Wydminy, Poland.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-24)

Source: https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESfQHrOzAVx9__Pgi6KKThAGLMKJjEJG9MNWjQj4P3R-0MUeSvyxQe_gke870nk3DG5XXv4mHUlW8r6y3K5QIj9I1nwv3KoeqCvDf8XkHfOETN5uWI_gdSYVw3_X3SZFfrbsYBHnl1qRvRYOK2muIj5zZTvAxUYzRswDlJEdtH
Title: Cittaslow through the lens of sustainable urban development: a comparative analysis of Italy and Türkiye cases
Chunks: 14,15,16,17,18
## 3. METHODOLOGY
### Table 2.  Results of context evaluation. Source: Author.
#### 3.1.3. Awareness of the urban fabric, local distinctiveness and local economy should be raised
Urban sustainability is related to the _urban fabric_ being handed down through generations. Toesca (1985) defined _urban fabric_ as ‘not just consist of the built structures, but also of the daily life within the built structures and in public spaces’ (Toesca (1985) definition of ‘Tessuto Urbano’ cited in Hoeschele, Citation 2010, p. 77). Specific attention to public spaces and town centres is vital for a sense of belonging. As Zagroba et al. (Citation 2021) mentioned, the town centre's limited size renders social integration an intrinsic element of its operation. Complementary criteria can be related to accessibility to city centres and social facilities and the promotion of mix-usage for the needs of inhabitants. Supporting mixed usages to create vibrant places for human interaction and safety is another essential aspect of urban sustainability (Jacobs, Citation 1961 ). There are specific supportive criteria for the urban fabric (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 3.2, 3.16, etc.) and mixed usage (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 3.15, 3.16). Another aspect is local distinctiveness. Protecting built heritage, local cultural events and traditional crafts will maintain the local identity (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 4.3, 4.7). Radstrom (Citation 2014) also emphasised that the main aim of Cittaslow is protecting the cities’ authenticity. Small towns gain a new characteristic when they become certified as Cittaslow (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 5.1, 5.3).

## 3. METHODOLOGY
### Table 2.  Results of context evaluation. Source: Author.
#### 3.1.3. Awareness of the urban fabric, local distinctiveness and local economy should be raised
Economic sustainability is also considered in several criteria: _4.2 Protection of handmade and labelled artisan production_, _4.3 Increasing the value of working techniques and traditional crafts_ and _4.5 Use of local products, if possible organic, in communal public restaurants_. Mayer and Knox (Citation 2006) explained that Cittaslow leverages local products to maintain the distinctiveness and sustainability of local economies, cultures and societies. This approach involves promoting and strengthening local entrepreneurship and creating new products that cater to local demand. By doing this, the character of products and services embedded in local traditions can be preserved (Brodziński & Kurowska, Citation 2021). Stimulating local businesses is one of the essential aspects of Cittaslow, and it should also include supporting their digitalisation. With the help of digitalisation, local entrepreneurs can expand their market nationally and even internationally.

## 3. METHODOLOGY
### 3.2. A comparison between two countries: Italy (Abbiategrasso) and Türkiye (Seferihisar)
Abbiategrasso is one of the small cities within the Milan Metropolitan Area. It connects with Milan and other cities through roads, railways and bike paths (see ). Its municipal boundary covers 47.05 km 2, with primarily agricultural land and parks; thus, the average density of Abbiategrasso is relatively low, with a value of 678 inhabitants per km 2. The history of Abbiategrasso is known from Roman times. There are many examples of civil architecture belonging to different periods, thanks to the rich history of Abbiategrasso. The old town centre is well protected, with the Castello Visconteo, ancient houses and churches dating back to the Renaissance and Baroque periods. The city's industrial sector is based on agriculture, with a primary focus on cultivating cereal crops, particularly rice and corn. Local products are vital for the economy of Abbiategrasso. In the Ticino Valley's rural communities, farmhouses produce stone-ground flour, old brands of wheat, cured meats, and renowned cheeses like Quartirolo and Gorgonzola.
Figure 1.  (a) Cittaslow network of Italy, (b) location of Abbiategrasso.
Source: Salieva Citation 2016.

## 3. METHODOLOGY
### 3.2. A comparison between two countries: Italy (Abbiategrasso) and Türkiye (Seferihisar)
Abbiategrasso was certificated as a Cittaslow in 2000. The population has increased from 27,760 to 32,681 since 2000. Based on the population statistics of Abbiategrasso, the percentage of foreign residents (11%) is almost equal to the Milan average (13%). There are limited sources for Cittaslow's candidacy process. A field trip and an interview with a local official helped create an understanding of the current situation in Abbiategrasso. During the field trip, it was observed that there are several Cittaslow symbols around the city, both on administrative buildings and on the shops’ windows on the main street (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 5.1, 5.3; see ). During the interview, the local official stated that Abbiategrasso was already a Cittaslow. During the candidacy period, particular projects are prepared to fulfil the requirements of Cittaslow certification. These projects include meeting with local shops and informing inhabitants, establishing a producer market for local agricultural products, creating a design code for streets and pedestrianising the main square, Piazza Guglielmo Marconi. These initiatives align with Cittaslow's criteria 2.4, 3.15, 4.2 and 4.3. The municipality also encourages local producers by supplying them with places to market their products (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 3.15) (Branduini & Carnelli, Citation 2021). In 2016, the municipality conducted a project to increase bicycle use and create a sustainable slow mobility system: the Bicipark project (Cittaslow International Project Prize, Citation 2016) (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4).
Figure 2.  (a) Castello Visconteo, (b) a Cafetteria on the Corso Matteotti Giacomo.
Source: Salieva Citation 2016.

## 3. METHODOLOGY
### 3.2. A comparison between two countries: Italy (Abbiategrasso) and Türkiye (Seferihisar)
The local official stated that Abbiategrasso became a Cittaslow to maintain its slow-living philosophy despite being close to Milan's city centre, where job opportunities are limited. For Abbiategrasso, Cittaslow can prevent the city's transformation into a sleeping town. Cittaslow has the ability to draw people in various ways and transform their perception of a small town. The city has improved its residents’ quality of life. On the other hand, there are some concerns as well. Nilsson et al. (Citation 2011) stated the local officials’ concerns about gentrification and the increasing number of new residents who commute daily to work in Milan.
Seferihisar is a small town in the western part of Türkiye. It is linked with Izmir by motorways; there is no railway link between them (see ). The current population density is relatively low (98 people per km 2) due to its broad territorial area that covers almost 370 square kilometres. Seferihisar has a rich historical background that has pioneered the process of becoming a Cittaslow. The oldest settlement in the Seferihisar is Teos, which was established around 2000 BC. Besides its rich historical background, it has unique products. Seferihisar’s tangerines are known on an international scale. Tangerine production is the primary source of income for inhabitants. Other imported agricultural products are olives and grapes. While agriculture is the leading sector, the second one is tourism. There are many summer houses close to the seaside.
Figure 3.  (a) Cittaslow network of Türkiye, (b) location of Seferihisar.
Source: Salieva Citation 2016.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

**Cittaslow** is an organisation founded in Italy and inspired by the slow food movement. Cittaslow's goals include improving the quality of life in towns by slowing down its overall pace, especially in a city's use of spaces and the flow of life and traffic through them.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-7)
As of November 2025, Cittaslow has 308 members, 221 in Europe, 71 in Asia, 6 in North America, 4 in South America, 4 in Oceania, and 2 in Africa. Countries with most members are Italy (90), Poland (37), Turkey (28), Germany (24), China (18), South Korea (15), France (13) and Spain (11).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-list-1)
texts.1:
Cittaslow was founded in Italy in October 1999, following a meeting organised by the mayor of Greve in Chianti, Tuscany.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-small_town_43-8) A 54-point charter was developed, encouraging high quality local food and drink, general conviviality and the opposition to cultural standardisation.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-small_town_43-8) In 2001, 28 Italian towns were signed up to the pledge, certified by trained operatives of Cittaslow.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-small_town_44-9)
The first Slow City in the English-speaking world was Ludlow, England, in 2003.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-Waking_up-10) In 2004, Reszel became the first Polish town to join Cittaslow, and several soon followed with the number growing to 12 by September 2013 and to 37 by November 2025, making Poland the country with the second highest number of member towns (after Italy).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-mkkg-11)
Welcome sign in Midden-Delfland, Netherlands, containing the Cittaslow logo. Midden-Delfland in 2008 was the first Dutch municipality to join[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-12)
The movement expanded broadly beyond Italy and, by 2006, national Cittaslow networks existed in Germany, Norway and the United Kingdom. In March 2007 the South Australian town of Goolwa was declared a Cittaslow member and became the first Non-European to gain Cittaslow membership_[citation needed_]. By 2007, several slow cities had been introduced across South Korea.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-13)
texts.2:
By mid-2009, fourteen countries had at least one officially accredited Cittaslow community. In July 2009, the small seaside village of Cowichan Bay in Canada became the North American continent's first Cittaslow town._[citation needed_] In June 2011, Gökçeada in Turkey became the first and only Cittaslow island.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-14) As of September 2013, Cittaslow had 177 members, the most in Italy (73), Poland, South Korea, Germany (12 each), Turkey (9) and France (8).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-mkkg-11)
In October 2020, Izmir, Turkey's 3rd metropolitan municipality, has become The First Cittaslow Metropolis of the World.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-15)
Cittaslow sign in Orneta, Poland
There are three categories of membership: Cittaslow town (population less than 50,000); Cittaslow Supporter (population more than 50,000);[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-16) and Cittaslow Friend (individual or family).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-17)
Like Slow Food, Cittaslow is a membership organisation. Full membership of Cittaslow is only open to towns with a population under 50,000. To become eligible for membership, a town must normally score at least 50 percent in a self-assessment process against the set of Cittaslow goals, and then apply for admission to the appropriate Cittaslow national network. An annual membership fee is payable by towns._[citation needed_]
texts.3:
The first town in England to become a Cittaslow city (and the first in the English-speaking world) was Ludlow[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-Waking_up-10) in November 2003;[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-research_themes_118-18) the first in Wales was Mold.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-research_themes_118-18) There are currently three towns in the UK that are members.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-uktowns-19)_[Disagrees with five named in the list._]
Pijao, a small town in Colombia, is to become the first Cittaslow city in Latin America.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-20)
Polish Cittaslow towns participate in the annual Cittaslow Towns Festival, hosted each year by a different member town in Poland.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-21) The first festival took place in 2010 in Reszel.
Some localitites withdrew from the organization, including Diss, UK, Fairfax, California, US, Ludlow, UK, Perth, UK, Taraklı, Turkey, and Wydminy, Poland.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cittaslow#cite_note-24)

## 3. METHODOLOGY
### Table 2.  Results of context evaluation. Source: Author.
#### 3.1.3. Awareness of the urban fabric, local distinctiveness and local economy should be raised
Urban sustainability is related to the _urban fabric_ being handed down through generations. Toesca (1985) defined _urban fabric_ as ‘not just consist of the built structures, but also of the daily life within the built structures and in public spaces’ (Toesca (1985) definition of ‘Tessuto Urbano’ cited in Hoeschele, Citation 2010, p. 77). Specific attention to public spaces and town centres is vital for a sense of belonging. As Zagroba et al. (Citation 2021) mentioned, the town centre's limited size renders social integration an intrinsic element of its operation. Complementary criteria can be related to accessibility to city centres and social facilities and the promotion of mix-usage for the needs of inhabitants. Supporting mixed usages to create vibrant places for human interaction and safety is another essential aspect of urban sustainability (Jacobs, Citation 1961 ). There are specific supportive criteria for the urban fabric (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 3.2, 3.16, etc.) and mixed usage (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 3.15, 3.16). Another aspect is local distinctiveness. Protecting built heritage, local cultural events and traditional crafts will maintain the local identity (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 4.3, 4.7). Radstrom (Citation 2014) also emphasised that the main aim of Cittaslow is protecting the cities’ authenticity. Small towns gain a new characteristic when they become certified as Cittaslow (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 5.1, 5.3).

## 3. METHODOLOGY
### Table 2.  Results of context evaluation. Source: Author.
#### 3.1.3. Awareness of the urban fabric, local distinctiveness and local economy should be raised
Economic sustainability is also considered in several criteria: _4.2 Protection of handmade and labelled artisan production_, _4.3 Increasing the value of working techniques and traditional crafts_ and _4.5 Use of local products, if possible organic, in communal public restaurants_. Mayer and Knox (Citation 2006) explained that Cittaslow leverages local products to maintain the distinctiveness and sustainability of local economies, cultures and societies. This approach involves promoting and strengthening local entrepreneurship and creating new products that cater to local demand. By doing this, the character of products and services embedded in local traditions can be preserved (Brodziński & Kurowska, Citation 2021). Stimulating local businesses is one of the essential aspects of Cittaslow, and it should also include supporting their digitalisation. With the help of digitalisation, local entrepreneurs can expand their market nationally and even internationally.

## 3. METHODOLOGY
### 3.2. A comparison between two countries: Italy (Abbiategrasso) and Türkiye (Seferihisar)
Abbiategrasso is one of the small cities within the Milan Metropolitan Area. It connects with Milan and other cities through roads, railways and bike paths (see ). Its municipal boundary covers 47.05 km 2, with primarily agricultural land and parks; thus, the average density of Abbiategrasso is relatively low, with a value of 678 inhabitants per km 2. The history of Abbiategrasso is known from Roman times. There are many examples of civil architecture belonging to different periods, thanks to the rich history of Abbiategrasso. The old town centre is well protected, with the Castello Visconteo, ancient houses and churches dating back to the Renaissance and Baroque periods. The city's industrial sector is based on agriculture, with a primary focus on cultivating cereal crops, particularly rice and corn. Local products are vital for the economy of Abbiategrasso. In the Ticino Valley's rural communities, farmhouses produce stone-ground flour, old brands of wheat, cured meats, and renowned cheeses like Quartirolo and Gorgonzola.
Figure 1.  (a) Cittaslow network of Italy, (b) location of Abbiategrasso.
Source: Salieva Citation 2016.

## 3. METHODOLOGY
### 3.2. A comparison between two countries: Italy (Abbiategrasso) and Türkiye (Seferihisar)
Abbiategrasso was certificated as a Cittaslow in 2000. The population has increased from 27,760 to 32,681 since 2000. Based on the population statistics of Abbiategrasso, the percentage of foreign residents (11%) is almost equal to the Milan average (13%). There are limited sources for Cittaslow's candidacy process. A field trip and an interview with a local official helped create an understanding of the current situation in Abbiategrasso. During the field trip, it was observed that there are several Cittaslow symbols around the city, both on administrative buildings and on the shops’ windows on the main street (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 5.1, 5.3; see ). During the interview, the local official stated that Abbiategrasso was already a Cittaslow. During the candidacy period, particular projects are prepared to fulfil the requirements of Cittaslow certification. These projects include meeting with local shops and informing inhabitants, establishing a producer market for local agricultural products, creating a design code for streets and pedestrianising the main square, Piazza Guglielmo Marconi. These initiatives align with Cittaslow's criteria 2.4, 3.15, 4.2 and 4.3. The municipality also encourages local producers by supplying them with places to market their products (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 3.15) (Branduini & Carnelli, Citation 2021). In 2016, the municipality conducted a project to increase bicycle use and create a sustainable slow mobility system: the Bicipark project (Cittaslow International Project Prize, Citation 2016) (Cittaslow, Citation 2022, Criterion 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4).
Figure 2.  (a) Castello Visconteo, (b) a Cafetteria on the Corso Matteotti Giacomo.
Source: Salieva Citation 2016.

## 3. METHODOLOGY
### 3.2. A comparison between two countries: Italy (Abbiategrasso) and Türkiye (Seferihisar)
The local official stated that Abbiategrasso became a Cittaslow to maintain its slow-living philosophy despite being close to Milan's city centre, where job opportunities are limited. For Abbiategrasso, Cittaslow can prevent the city's transformation into a sleeping town. Cittaslow has the ability to draw people in various ways and transform their perception of a small town. The city has improved its residents’ quality of life. On the other hand, there are some concerns as well. Nilsson et al. (Citation 2011) stated the local officials’ concerns about gentrification and the increasing number of new residents who commute daily to work in Milan.
Seferihisar is a small town in the western part of Türkiye. It is linked with Izmir by motorways; there is no railway link between them (see ). The current population density is relatively low (98 people per km 2) due to its broad territorial area that covers almost 370 square kilometres. Seferihisar has a rich historical background that has pioneered the process of becoming a Cittaslow. The oldest settlement in the Seferihisar is Teos, which was established around 2000 BC. Besides its rich historical background, it has unique products. Seferihisar’s tangerines are known on an international scale. Tangerine production is the primary source of income for inhabitants. Other imported agricultural products are olives and grapes. While agriculture is the leading sector, the second one is tourism. There are many summer houses close to the seaside.
Figure 3.  (a) Cittaslow network of Türkiye, (b) location of Seferihisar.

## The Monumental Nativity Scene of the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### The living models of the Monumental Nativity
This is the part visitors remember years later. For Saint Joseph, Sirio, the sculptor's son, posed. For the Assyrian King, Erminio Spalla posed, the boxer, European heavyweight champion in the 1920s and later an actor and singer: a body Ferri wanted because it held up the monumental scale without looking bloated. For the Indian King, an 80-year-old resident of the Cottolengo of Don Orione posed, while for the head of the same Indian King the artist used himself. Knowing that inside a nativity scene 4 meters high there are a professional boxer, an elderly man in care and the author's son completely changes the way you look at it.

## The Monumental Nativity Scene of the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### How the Madonna and Saint Joseph came about
The first version of the Madonna and Saint Joseph convinced neither the artist nor the patrons. Ferri redid them in 60 days of uninterrupted work, modeling even at night under harsh lights to check the sculptural effects, that is to see how the shadows would work once the piece was placed high up and lit from below. The stated aim was to detach the material world, represented by the Magi with their trappings of wealth, and to exalt the spiritual world with the Virgin's purest and simplest lines. Look at the drapery: the Magi's is agitated, broken, full of undercuts. Mary's is continuous, almost smooth. The difference is not stylistic, it's theological.

## The Monumental Nativity Scene of the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### Why the Monumental Nativity ended up in Cave
The nativity scene never reached Sant'Andrea della Valle. The economic difficulties of the postwar period made the Pallottines lose interest in the project, and in 1952 the work was inaugurated in the crypt of the Regina Pacis basilica, in Ostia. In December 2012 the whole complex was moved and set up in the vast underground space of the former Augustinian convent, adjacent to the town hall, in the historic center of Cave: a cross-vaulted space that, for once, seems built for the purpose. The link between Ferri and Cave, as we'll see, was not accidental, and the town inherited a work that Rome had commissioned and then let drop.

## The Shroud studies at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
The room devoted to the Shroud studies, in the former Augustinian convent, reconstructs the atmosphere of the Shroud room of Ferri's Roman studio and documents 46 years of research. It is the part of the museum that divides visitors, and it should be said up front for clarity: Ferri was not a theologian and the museum does not issue verdicts on the authenticity of the Turin cloth. Ferri was a sculptor who applied the tools of artistic anatomy to the image on the Shroud, with the same stubbornness with which he had reassembled a Hellenistic group from fragments.

## The Shroud studies at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### Lorenzo Ferri's method
Ferri began working on the Shroud in the late 1920s, working from Giuseppe Enrie's photographic plates, and did not stop until his death. In 1950 he presented his artistic and scientific material at the First International Congress on the Holy Shroud. In 1952 he was received in private audience by Pius XII, to whom he presented the face of Jesus reconstructed from the imprint. In 1951 he reached the insight on which everything else rests: that the imprints on the cloth contained three-dimensional information, that is that the intensity of the image varied according to the distance between the body and the fabric. From that idea came the two sculptural reconstructions, the RP1 in resin made between 1966 and 1968, 198 centimeters tall, and the RP2 in plaster worked between 1972 and 1975, 197 centimeters tall, in addition to the 1972 reconstruction of the scourging and the 1974 one of the skull. From his measurements Ferri derived a height of around 1.85 meters, an S-shaped position of the body and a dislocation of the left shoulder.

## The Shroud studies at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### The faces, the hands, the feet
The room displays the series of faces in chronological order, and the sequence is the most instructive thing in the whole museum. The 1933 Borgongini face in patinated terracotta, the 1937-1938 Christus face in patinated plaster, the 1951 Spinelli face in marble and in the painted plaster version, the 1954 Felbermayer face, the 1966 Vitt face in wax and the half-closed-eyes one of 1961, the Shroud face with barely sketched hair of 1970 in terracotta, the scourged face of 1971 in painted plaster. Alongside, the pairs of hands and feet divided into a first manner, of 1950-1960, and a second manner, of 1967-1968, in plaster and in resin: the revision of an anatomical detail carried out over 15 years.
Then there is a collection you don't expect and that throws you off: the death masks. Cavour, Trilussa, Mazzini, Tolstoy, Beethoven, Monsignor Borgongini Duca, Valtorta. Ferri studied them to understand how the human face changes after death, and displayed them next to the 1973 cadaveric Shroud face RP2. It's a room to be looked at with a steady stomach and without sentimentality: it's a laboratory, not a chapel.

## The Shroud studies at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### The other pieces in the Shroud room
The room is completed by the cloth with the 1964 reproduction of the Shroud, 4.36 by 1.50 meters. The large oil on canvas "Jesus nailed to the cross on the ground" of 1953-1961, 247 by 122 centimeters. The graph of the axis of symmetry of the face, charcoal on paper of 1949. The living Shroud face in charcoal of 1958. The Shroud crucifix in plaster on wood of 1952 at one-quarter scale. The four bronze figures of the phases of the deposition from the cross of 1974. And the high-relief bust of 1972 with the dislocated shoulder. In the same room are displayed the original sketches for the Janua Coeli door, those of 1968-1970 in full-size plaster, 226 by 520 centimeters, and the two sketches in patinated plaster of 1970.

## The upper room of the former convent: Fallani, Saint Francis and Jakarta
The upper room of the former convent of the Augustinian friars displays works made between 1950 and 1965 and, a rare and generous gesture, some works by Ferri's teacher, Giuseppe Fallani (1859-1933): the four plaster sketches submitted to the third competition for the Palace of Justice in Rome, that is "Strength", "Justice", "Charity" and "The Law", all from 1898, and a plaster "Venus" of 1904. Seeing the teacher next to the pupil, in a museum named for the pupil, is a museum choice that no great museum would allow itself and that works very well here.
Part of the same room are the sketches for the nativity scene of Sant'Andrea della Valle, that is the preparatory models of the statues you see at full scale in the underground space: the kneeling Indian King, the Madonna with the Child in two versions, Saint Joseph, the page, the Assyrian King with page. Going from the sketches to the statues is an exercise I recommend doing in the right order, first the small and then the large.

## The upper room of the former convent: Fallani, Saint Francis and Jakarta
Then there is the Franciscan group commissioned by Bishop Cristoforo Arduino Terzi to enhance the Franciscan sites of the Rieti valley: the "Saint Francis and the wolf" of 1958, "Brother Masseo lying down", "Brother Angelo with the lute", "Saint Francis declaiming the Canticle of the Creatures", "Brother Bernardino kneeling", "Brother Leo writing the rule", all between 1960 and 1964, and the detail of the head of Saint Francis of 1972. Anyone who knows the sanctuaries of the Rieti valley recognizes the project right away. The room is completed by the Immaculate Conception in a ceramic mandorla of 1965, the monstrance with Saint Francis and a glory of angels of 1958, the seven holy founders of the Servite order, the plaster copy of the Sarcophagus of the Spouses of 1950 and the series of sketches for the national monument in Jakarta of 1964, with the ship, the young man with the bow, the Indonesian bull and the eagle emblem of Indonesia, of which there is also an imposing plaster detail of the head, 76 by 16 by 105 centimeters.

## Lorenzo Ferri and the town of Cave: the Veronica, the bronze door, the Crucifix
There remains the question everyone asks on arriving: why a museum dedicated to a sculptor from Romagna, who lived and died in Rome, is in a town in the Monti Prenestini. The answer has a first and last name, Monsignor Lorenzo Castellani, parish priest of Cave. Ferri, for his Shroud studies, frequented Roman ecclesiastical circles, and there he became friends with Castellani, who brought him to Cave.
The first work for the town is a canvas of the Veronica with the face of Christ crowned with thorns, made for the Pro-Good Friday Committee of which Castellani was spiritual director, today kept in the church of Santa Maria Assunta. Two works followed that tell of by now an affectionate relationship: the bronze door of the same church of Santa Maria Assunta, the Janua Coeli, presented in 1970 to Paul VI and inaugurated in 1972, which illustrates the life of the Virgin and in which Ferri himself and Monsignor Castellani are portrayed. And the Shroud Crucifix, begun in 1964 and cast in bronze after the artist's death, displayed in the hamlet of San Bartolomeo.
A practical tip worth the time it costs: after visiting the museum, go up to the collegiate church of Santa Maria Assunta and look at the door. It's a few minutes' walk from Palazzo Comunale, has no ticket and closes the circle, because in the gypsotheca you saw the full-size plasters and the sketches, and here you see the bronze mounted on its hinges, with the figures of the two friends who slipped into the story of the Virgin like the donors in the polyptychs of the 1400s.

## The Trilussa monument and Lorenzo Ferri's Roman works
Lorenzo Ferri's most famous piece is not in a museum: it's in Trastevere, in Piazza Trilussa, and it's the monument to the poet. In 1952, after a heated debate in the City Council, the square until then known as Piazza di Ponte Sisto was named after Carlo Alberto Salustri, that is Trilussa, who died in 1950. The monument, with a base in brick facing and ancient architectural elements and with the bronze bust, was inaugurated on December 22, 1954 in the presence of a large crowd and of Mayor Salvatore Rebecchini. Running along the monument are the verses of "All'ombra": "Mentre me leggo er solito giornale / spaparacchiato all'ombra d'un pajaro" and the closing "de poté dì le cose come stanno / senza paura de finì in priggione".
Ferri had never portrayed Trilussa from life. He worked from photographs and from the descriptions of Rosa Tomei, the woman who had been at the poet's side. In the gypsotheca at Cave you can see the bust in patinated plaster and the full-length figure in small format, that is the two stages of that portrait built through someone else's memory. It's a fact that restores professional dignity to a monument that Romans treat as a place to rest their beers on a Saturday night: that face is a work of reconstruction, not a copy.
Among Ferri's Roman works is also the Christ the Redeemer of the Prima Porta cemetery, the Flaminio cemetery, a monumental marble statue 4 meters high worked on between 1961 and 1973: his ashes rest at the foot of that statue. And there is the chapter of the competition for the bronze doors of St. Peter's Basilica, in which Ferri was a finalist in 1948 with a sketch for the second level. The reliefs can be seen in the gypsotheca. He lost, as almost everyone lost, but the fact that an art teacher from the public school system reached the final of that competition says how much his hand was worth. To get your bearings in the rest of the capital's museum landscape you can start from the page devoted to the museums of Rome.

## Knock, Jakarta and Lorenzo Ferri's international commissions
Between 1960 and 1963 Ferri made the marble Apparition group for the shrine of Knock, in County Mayo, Ireland. The shrine describes the statues as executed in very white Carrara marble, commissioned by the Knock Shrine Society, with the Virgin at the center, Saint John the Evangelist on her right and Saint Joseph on her left, following the account of the 15 witnesses of the 1879 apparition and the interviews of the 1930s with Mary Byrne O'Connell. In the chapel an altar with the Lamb and sculpted angels completes the scene. It is one of the most visited pilgrimage destinations in Europe, and almost all of the millions of people who pass through are unaware that the author is an Italian whose preparatory plasters are on the second floor of a former hospital in a town in the Monti Prenestini.
Between 1964 and 1966 Ferri worked on the bronze portal and the statues for the Independence Shrine in Jakarta. In 1963 he made mosaics and stained glass for the church of the Comboni Missionaries in Rome. In 1970 he received the prize of Accademia Tiberina and was named a Tiberine academician. He made the medal for the centenary of Rome as capital. The three-dimensional reconstruction of the face of the Man of the Shroud was published in the volume "L'uomo della Sindone nella ricostruzione dello scultore Lorenzo Ferri", published by Kappa in 2012.

## A curiosity about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
Inside the Monumental Nativity there is a boxer. The Assyrian King, the figure that together with his page occupies a front of 3.60 meters, has the body of Erminio Spalla, who in the 1920s had been European heavyweight champion and who later turned to film and song. Ferri didn't choose him for his name: he needed a physique able to hold up the monumental scale without becoming a muscular caricature, and a professional boxer, trained to stay balanced, was the technical solution. In the same group an 80-year-old resident of the Cottolengo of Don Orione posed as the Indian King, while Saint Joseph is modeled on Sirio, the sculptor's son, and the head of the Indian King is Ferri's own.
Lined up, the thing is something of a marvel: in front of the Epiphany at Cave you find a sports champion, an elderly man assisted by a charitable work, a son and the author. A catalog of real men dressed as kings. It's the kind of information that changes the way you look at a work, because it dismantles the idea that 20th-century sacred sculpture was made of ideal models. Ferri worked exactly like the painters of the 1600s who picked their apostles out of the tavern, and the result is that those nine figures, despite their height, have believable flesh. Look at the Assyrian King's hands: they are hands with the knuckles of someone who has hit something.

## Something nobody tells you about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
Nobody will tell you that the most famous piece of this museum is not in the museum, and that millions of people have already seen it without knowing they've seen it. The monument to Trilussa in Piazza Trilussa, in Trastevere, the one the kids sit under on Saturday night, is by Lorenzo Ferri and was inaugurated on December 22, 1954. At Cave are kept the bust in patinated plaster and the figure in small format, that is the two preparatory stages.
The detail nobody tells is how that face came about. Ferri had never had Trilussa in front of him: the poet had died in 1950 and the square was named for him in 1952, after a heated debate in the City Council. The sculptor worked from photographs and from the descriptions of Rosa Tomei, the woman who had been at his side. Reconstructing a face from flat images and verbal testimony is exactly the technical problem Ferri was tackling, in the same years, on the imprint of the Shroud. The most popular monument in Trastevere and the most solitary research of his life are the same exercise applied to two different materials.
I'll add a second thing that is almost never written: in the upper room of the former convent are displayed four sketches from 1898 by Giuseppe Fallani, Ferri's teacher, submitted to the competition for the Palace of Justice in Rome. A monographic museum that displays its own teacher is a gesture of intellectual honesty worth the detour.

## The advice I give you for visiting the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
Call. Before anything else, call 06 5745934 and book, because the museum works by appointment and the hours undergo seasonal changes. Having done that, organize the visit the opposite way from how almost everyone does it: start from the gypsotheca on Via Cavour, go up to the second floor, and only afterward go down into the underground space of the former convent for the Monumental Nativity. Whoever does the reverse route sees the twist first and then gets bored in front of the small plasters. Whoever does it in this order arrives in front of the nine statues having already seen the 20-centimeter sketches, and understands what it means to take a small model to 4 meters.
Second piece of advice: take the afternoon slot, from 16:30 to 19:30. It's three hours against the scant two of the morning, and it leaves you time to go up to the collegiate church of Santa Maria Assunta to see the bronze door Janua Coeli mounted on its hinges, after having looked at its full-size plaster sketches in the Shroud room. The circle closes there, not in the museum.
Third piece of advice, the most unwelcome: don't dispatch the Shroud room in three minutes because the subject leaves you cold. It's the most original part of the collection and can be looked at perfectly well as a chapter of 20th-century artistic anatomy, without subscribing to anything. The sequence of faces from 1933 to 1973, one next to the other, is a document on the sculptor's craft that has few equivalents in Italy.

## Another well-known fact, yet rarely cited
Everyone says the Monumental Nativity was born for Sant'Andrea della Valle. What is rarely cited is the consequence: that nativity scene never arrived in Rome. The competition was announced by the Pallottine Fathers in 1946 to renew the nativity scene donated by the Torlonia family, on the occasion of the centenary of the Epiphany Octave established by Saint Vincent Pallotti. Ferri won, calculated the proportions on the double-square rectangle of the church and designed a placement in front of the apse, 3 meters above the floor. Then the economic penury of the postwar period made the patrons lose interest, and the work was left without a home.
In 1952 the nativity scene was inaugurated in the crypt of the Regina Pacis basilica, in Ostia, where it stayed for 60 years. Only in December 2012 were the nine statues moved and set up in the underground space of the former Augustinian convent, next to the town hall of Cave. The complete journey, then, is this: commissioned for the second tallest church in Rome, displayed in a crypt on the coast, finally relocated to a town in the Monti Prenestini.
There's a moral in this story. Works of art don't end up where they should: they end up where someone decides to take care of them. Cave took on a work that Rome had ordered and then let go, built a cross-vaulted space around it and put its author's name on the door. A €3 ticket is the rest of the story.

## The right photo to take at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
The right photo is just one and it's taken in the underground space of the former convent: stand at the feet of Saint Joseph, the statue the catalog records at 384.7 centimeters in height, and frame from below looking up, keeping in the field the springing of the cross vault. The contrast between the cut of the ribs and the figure's drapery does the work by itself, and the perspective distortion that usually ruins photos is here exactly what conveys the real scale. If you have someone with you, have them step into the low corner of the frame: without a human figure nobody will believe the proportions.
The second photo to take home is something else entirely. In the Shroud studies room, the sequence of faces arranged in chronological order should be photographed edge-on, not head-on: a row of heads from 1933 to 1973, in terracotta, in marble, in plaster, in wax, repeating the same subject 40 times with 40 different outcomes. It's the image that explains the museum better than any caption.
Two technical warnings. The first: the light here is that of rooms carved out of historic buildings, so keep the sensitivity high and resign yourself to giving up the flash, which on white plaster flattens all the modeling and destroys exactly what you came to see. The second: the rules on filming, tripods and professional use of images are set by the museum, and in a small venue they are agreed simply by asking the staff when you book.

## Some important events that took place here in history
Cave has a date that appears in the textbooks of modern history: September 14, 1557. During the Salt War, the conflict that pitted Pope Paul IV Carafa and his French allies against the Spain of Philip II, the final negotiations took place right here and the peace was signed at Cave. It was the end of the papacy's last great military adventure in Italy and the beginning of a long Spanish predominance over the peninsula: a treaty signed in a hill town that closes a European chapter.
The events concerning the museum are more recent and can be counted on one hand. In 1946 the Pallottine Fathers announce the competition for the nativity scene, which Ferri wins. The nine statues are sculpted between 1947 and 1948. In 1952 the Monumental Nativity is inaugurated in the crypt of the Regina Pacis basilica in Ostia, and in the same year Ferri is received in private audience by Pius XII, to whom he presents the face reconstructed from the imprint of the Shroud. In 1970 the bronze door Janua Coeli is presented to Paul VI. It is inaugurated on the church of Santa Maria Assunta in Cave in 1972. In 1975 Ferri dies in Rome.
Then come the dates of memory. The heirs donate the collection of works to the Municipality of Cave. On May 30, 2013 Museo Civico "Città di Cave" is established. In December 2012 the Monumental Nativity section opens in the underground space of the former Augustinian convent. On December 7, 2013 the gypsotheca opens in the former Mattei Hospital. In 2024 the museum joins the Museum System of the Castelli Romani and Prenestini.

## Who has been through the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
The people who have left a trace in this museum, in plaster or in bronze, make up an improbable list. There are two pontiffs: Pius XII, who in 1952 received Ferri in private audience and saw the face reconstructed from the Shroud, and Paul VI, to whom in 1970 the bronze door for the church of Cave was presented. Of John XXIII, four medal molds from 1963 are kept. There is Monsignor Lorenzo Castellani, parish priest of Cave, the man for whom everything else exists: without his friendship the sculptor would never have set foot in this town.
There are portraits of the great: Giovanni Giolitti in 1959, Antonio Rosmini in 1956, Luciano Manara, Ennio Quirino Visconti, Cardinal Lepicier in 1930, Cardinal Borgongini Duca, Monsignor Ferdinando Baldelli in 1972, and of course Trilussa. There are the death masks of Cavour, Mazzini, Tolstoy and Beethoven, which Ferri studied to understand how a face changes after death. There is Erminio Spalla, the boxer turned Assyrian King.
And then there are the two names that matter most for the artist's story. Giuseppe Fallani, restorer of the Sacred Apostolic Palaces, Ferri's teacher when he was a boy, whose 1898 sketches for the Palace of Justice and a Venus of 1904 are displayed in the upper room. And Alberto Carlo Carpiceci, favorite pupil and later brother-in-law, who collaborated on the Monumental Nativity. A museum that displays the teacher and the pupil next to the author tells of a craft, not a career.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### Where is the Lorenzo Ferri Museum?
The main section is at Via Cavour 23, 00033 Cave, in the province of Rome, in the building of the former Mattei Hospital. The Monumental Nativity section is in the underground rooms of Palazzo Comunale, the former convent of the Augustinians, in the historic center.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### What are the Lorenzo Ferri Museum's hours?
Closed Monday and Tuesday. Wednesday to Sunday from 10:30 to 12:30 and from 16:30 to 19:30. The ticket office closes 30 minutes before closing time. Hours may vary with the seasons, so it's best to confirm when you book.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### Do you need to book to visit the Lorenzo Ferri Museum?
Yes. The museum is visited by reservation, through the form on the official website or by calling 06 5745934.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### How much is a ticket to the Lorenzo Ferri Museum?
Full price €3, reduced €2.50. The reduced rate applies to residents, to groups of over 20 people, to children and young people from 3 to 18 years old and to those over 65.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### Who gets in free at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum?
People with disabilities with a companion, and children up to 3 years old.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### Is the Lorenzo Ferri Museum public or private?
It is a civic museum, of the Municipality of Cave, and forms a section of Museo Civico "Città di Cave".

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### What is the Lorenzo Ferri Museum's phone number?
06 5745934. The museum's email address is museolorenzoferri@gmail.com. The switchboard of the Municipality of Cave answers at 06 9500081.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### Who was Lorenzo Ferri?
A sculptor, painter, restorer, Shroud scholar and teacher born in Mercato Saraceno on July 18, 1902 and died in Rome on February 25, 1975. He trained in Rome in the workshop of Giuseppe Fallani, graduated from Istituto di Belle Arti in 1921 and worked in Argentina, in Libya, in Campania and in Basilicata before settling permanently in the capital.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### How long does it take to visit the Lorenzo Ferri Museum?
An hour and a half for the gypsotheca at a relaxed pace, 40 minutes for the Monumental Nativity. Three hours if you want to see both sections and go up to the collegiate church for the bronze door.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### How many statues does the Monumental Nativity of Cave have?
Nine, in plaster, sculpted between 1947 and 1948: the Madonna with the Child, Saint Joseph, the three Magi and their respective pages.

## Quick questions about the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### How tall are the statues of the Monumental Nativity?
The standing figures come close to 4 meters: the catalog records Saint Joseph at 384.7 centimeters, the Assyrian King with page at 375.5, the African King at 370.2 and the seated Madonna with the Child at 367.1. The kneeling figures exceed two and a half meters.

## The Monumental Nativity Scene of the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### The living models of the Monumental Nativity
This is the part visitors remember years later. For Saint Joseph, Sirio, the sculptor's son, posed. For the Assyrian King, Erminio Spalla posed, the boxer, European heavyweight champion in the 1920s and later an actor and singer: a body Ferri wanted because it held up the monumental scale without looking bloated. For the Indian King, an 80-year-old resident of the Cottolengo of Don Orione posed, while for the head of the same Indian King the artist used himself. Knowing that inside a nativity scene 4 meters high there are a professional boxer, an elderly man in care and the author's son completely changes the way you look at it.
texts.14:
## The Monumental Nativity Scene of the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### How the Madonna and Saint Joseph came about
The first version of the Madonna and Saint Joseph convinced neither the artist nor the patrons. Ferri redid them in 60 days of uninterrupted work, modeling even at night under harsh lights to check the sculptural effects, that is to see how the shadows would work once the piece was placed high up and lit from below. The stated aim was to detach the material world, represented by the Magi with their trappings of wealth, and to exalt the spiritual world with the Virgin's purest and simplest lines. Look at the drapery: the Magi's is agitated, broken, full of undercuts. Mary's is continuous, almost smooth. The difference is not stylistic, it's theological.
texts.15:
## The Monumental Nativity Scene of the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### Why the Monumental Nativity ended up in Cave
The nativity scene never reached Sant'Andrea della Valle. The economic difficulties of the postwar period made the Pallottines lose interest in the project, and in 1952 the work was inaugurated in the crypt of the Regina Pacis basilica, in Ostia. In December 2012 the whole complex was moved and set up in the vast underground space of the former Augustinian convent, adjacent to the town hall, in the historic center of Cave: a cross-vaulted space that, for once, seems built for the purpose. The link between Ferri and Cave, as we'll see, was not accidental, and the town inherited a work that Rome had commissioned and then let drop.
texts.16:
## The Shroud studies at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
The room devoted to the Shroud studies, in the former Augustinian convent, reconstructs the atmosphere of the Shroud room of Ferri's Roman studio and documents 46 years of research. It is the part of the museum that divides visitors, and it should be said up front for clarity: Ferri was not a theologian and the museum does not issue verdicts on the authenticity of the Turin cloth. Ferri was a sculptor who applied the tools of artistic anatomy to the image on the Shroud, with the same stubbornness with which he had reassembled a Hellenistic group from fragments.
texts.17:
## The Shroud studies at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### Lorenzo Ferri's method
Ferri began working on the Shroud in the late 1920s, working from Giuseppe Enrie's photographic plates, and did not stop until his death. In 1950 he presented his artistic and scientific material at the First International Congress on the Holy Shroud. In 1952 he was received in private audience by Pius XII, to whom he presented the face of Jesus reconstructed from the imprint. In 1951 he reached the insight on which everything else rests: that the imprints on the cloth contained three-dimensional information, that is that the intensity of the image varied according to the distance between the body and the fabric. From that idea came the two sculptural reconstructions, the RP1 in resin made between 1966 and 1968, 198 centimeters tall, and the RP2 in plaster worked between 1972 and 1975, 197 centimeters tall, in addition to the 1972 reconstruction of the scourging and the 1974 one of the skull. From his measurements Ferri derived a height of around 1.85 meters, an S-shaped position of the body and a dislocation of the left shoulder.
texts.18:
## The Shroud studies at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### The faces, the hands, the feet
The room displays the series of faces in chronological order, and the sequence is the most instructive thing in the whole museum. The 1933 Borgongini face in patinated terracotta, the 1937-1938 Christus face in patinated plaster, the 1951 Spinelli face in marble and in the painted plaster version, the 1954 Felbermayer face, the 1966 Vitt face in wax and the half-closed-eyes one of 1961, the Shroud face with barely sketched hair of 1970 in terracotta, the scourged face of 1971 in painted plaster. Alongside, the pairs of hands and feet divided into a first manner, of 1950-1960, and a second manner, of 1967-1968, in plaster and in resin: the revision of an anatomical detail carried out over 15 years.
Then there is a collection you don't expect and that throws you off: the death masks. Cavour, Trilussa, Mazzini, Tolstoy, Beethoven, Monsignor Borgongini Duca, Valtorta. Ferri studied them to understand how the human face changes after death, and displayed them next to the 1973 cadaveric Shroud face RP2. It's a room to be looked at with a steady stomach and without sentimentality: it's a laboratory, not a chapel.
texts.19:
## The Shroud studies at the Lorenzo Ferri Museum
### The other pieces in the Shroud room
The room is completed by the cloth with the 1964 reproduction of the Shroud, 4.36 by 1.50 meters. The large oil on canvas "Jesus nailed to the cross on the ground" of 1953-1961, 247 by 122 centimeters. The graph of the axis of symmetry of the face, charcoal on paper of 1949. The living Shroud face in charcoal of 1958. The Shroud crucifix in plaster on wood of 1952 at one-quarter scale. The four bronze figures of the phases of the deposition from the cross of 1974. And the high-relief bust of 1972 with the dislocated shoulder. In the same room are displayed the original sketches for the Janua Coeli door, those of 1968-1970 in full-size plaster, 226 by 520 centimeters, and the two sketches in patinated plaster of 1970.
texts.20:
## The upper room of the former convent: Fallani, Saint Francis and Jakarta
The upper room of the former convent of the Augustinian friars displays works made between 1950 and 1965 and, a rare and generous gesture, some works by Ferri's teacher, Giuseppe Fallani (1859-1933): the four plaster sketches submitted to the third competition for the Palace of Justice in Rome, that is "Strength", "Justice", "Charity" and "The Law", all from 1898, and a plaster "Venus" of 1904. Seeing the teacher next to the pupil, in a museum named for the pupil, is a museum choice that no great museum would allow itself and that works very well here.
Part of the same room are the sketches for the nativity scene of Sant'Andrea della Valle, that is the preparatory models of the statues you see at full scale in the underground space: the kneeling Indian King, the Madonna with the Child in two versions, Saint Joseph, the page, the Assyrian King with page. Going from the sketches to the statues is an exercise I recommend doing in the right order, first the small and then the large.
texts.21:
## The upper room of the former convent: Fallani, Saint Francis and Jakarta
Then there is the Franciscan group commissioned by Bishop Cristoforo Arduino Terzi to enhance the Franciscan sites of the Rieti valley: the "Saint Francis and the wolf" of 1958, "Brother Masseo lying down", "Brother Angelo with the lute", "Saint Francis declaiming the Canticle of the Creatures", "Brother Bernardino kneeling", "Brother Leo writing the rule", all between 1960 and 1964, and the detail of the head of Saint Francis of 1972. Anyone who knows the sanctuaries of the Rieti valley recognizes the project right away. The room is completed by the Immaculate Conception in a ceramic mandorla of 1965, the monstrance with Saint Francis and a glory of angels of 1958, the seven holy founders of the Servite order, the plaster copy of the Sarcophagus of the Spouses of 1950 and the series of sketches for the national monument in Jakarta of 1964, with the ship, the young man with the bow, the Indonesian bull and the eagle emblem of Indonesia, of which there is also an imposing plaster detail of the head, 76 by 16 by 105 centimeters.

## Lorenzo Ferri and the town of Cave: the Veronica, the bronze door, the Crucifix
There remains the question everyone asks on arriving: why a museum dedicated to a sculptor from Romagna, who lived and died in Rome, is in a town in the Monti Prenestini. The answer has a first and last name, Monsignor Lorenzo Castellani, parish priest of Cave. Ferri, for his Shroud studies, frequented Roman ecclesiastical circles, and there he became friends with Castellani, who brought him to Cave.
The first work for the town is a canvas of the Veronica with the face of Christ crowned with thorns, made for the Pro-Good Friday Committee of which Castellani was spiritual director, today kept in the church of Santa Maria Assunta. Two works followed that tell of by now an affectionate relationship: the bronze door of the same church of Santa Maria Assunta, the Janua Coeli, presented in 1970 to Paul VI and inaugurated in 1972, which illustrates the life of the Virgin and in which Ferri himself and Monsignor Castellani are portrayed.
